transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Ava Martinez (Redwood AE), Liam Chen (Redwood SE), Maya Singh (OptiRetail CTO), Jon Park (Lead ML Eng), Priya Patel (Infra/SRE), Carlos Ruiz (Security)\n\nSummary:
Quick technical deep dive to help OptiRetail decide between Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private (VPC/on-prem) for latency-sensitive inference workloads. Focus areas: runtime performance, latency/throughput tradeoffs, KV cache behavior, batching strategies, quantization impacts, noisy-neighbor isolation, and throughput guarantees. End with next steps and who supplies which artifacts for benchmarks.\n\nTopics:
- Baseline latency and p99 targets
- Throughput vs cost with batching
- KV cache hit patterns and warmup behavior
- Quantization tradeoffs (int8/llm.int8/4-bit)
- Dedicated isolation, noisy neighbor mitigation, capacity guarantees
- VPC/on-prem deployment concerns (KMS, audit logs, network egress)\n\nTranscript body:
[00:00] Ava: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — I'm Ava from Redwood, AE for you're account, and Liam our SE will run the deep dive. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Maya: Hey Ava, doing good, thanks. We are super keen to understand the perf tradeoffs here because our storefront uses real-time generation for product descriptions and chat help. Latency matters.
[00:12] Jon: Yeah hi, Jon here. Our p95 needs to be under 250ms for most interactive flows, p99 ideally under 500ms. We also have nightly batch embedding jobs but primary is latency-sensitive.
[00:20] Liam: Great, that's helpful. Quick upfront, do you have an approximate token distribution and sequence length? e.g. median seq length, and typical prompt sizes.
[00:28] Jon: Typical prompts are ~60-120 tokens, responses around 80-200 tokens. But we also have a small set of long-form summaries 1-2k tokens.
[00:36] Priya: And to flag from infra/security: we need VPC deployment if we go dedicated or on-prem; SOC2 and single-tenant audit logs are a must. Also curious about KMS integration.
[00:47] Ava: Yep, we support VPC/private with customer-managed KMS and full audit logs. We'll share the SOC2 pack.
[00:52] [00:52] Speaker 1 (Liam): Alright, I'll start with runtime fundamentals then get into KV cache and batching. First: hosted vs dedicated — hosted is multi-tenant with soft isolation, optimistic routing, autoscaling; dedicated gives reserved GPU pools for your tenants with guaranteed capacity and stricter network isolation. The tradeoff usually is cost vs guarantees.
[01:12] Jon: By "soft isolation" do you mean noisy neighbor could affect our p99? How often does that happen on hosted?
[01:17] Liam: Good question — on hosted we mitigate with request-level routing and fair-queueing, but you can see transient p99 spikes if there are bursty workloads in the same pool. For most customers it's rare, but for strict p99 SLOs we recommend Dedicated or Private so you have reserved inferencing capacity.
[01:33] Maya: For Dedicated, are we talking single-tenant GPUs or shared racks? We need isolation for compliance.
[01:38] Liam: Dedicated provides isolated GPU pools per customer, you get reserved nodes that are effectively single-tenant for inference. Network can be VPC peered or private link. For on-prem we can do air-gapped with customer runtime.
[01:47] Carlos: And latency-wise, do you have throughput guarantees? We need spiky traffic guarantees as well — Black Friday style spikes.
[01:53] Ava: Dedicated is backed by commit contracts with throughput targeting and can include burst capacity options. We can model expected QPS and define guaranteed throughput with a buffer.
[02:02] Liam: Now about runtime performance — our engine does continuous batching with kernel selection per model/sequence length. That gives low per-token overhead for small sequences while allowing high throughput for batched requests. The trick is latency vs throughput tuning: small batch sizes reduce tail latency; larger batches increase throughput but raise latency.
[02:20] Jon: Can you run numbers? Say we have 100 QPS with avg 120 tokens per call, what's p99 on hosted vs dedicated?
[02:27] Liam: Ballpark: on dedicated with proper batching knobs and KV cache, you'd see p50 around 60-80ms for short completions, p95 ~150-200ms, p99 ~300-400ms depending on model and quantization. Hosted is similar for median but p99 can be 20-50% higher in bursty periods. Those are high level — we'll run targeted benchmarks with your trace.
[02:46] Maya: You said KV cache — how big of a difference does that make for us? We do lots of small follow-ups in session.
[02:52] Liam: KV cache reduces autoregressive compute dramatically for sessioned conversations. If you have high locality in prompts (same conversation), cache hits can reduce token compute by 60-90% after warmup. Warmup behavior matters: first requests are cold and then the KV gets populated; cache eviction policy also matters — LRU vs policy that weights recent conversations.
[03:12] Jon: How do you handle cache coherence in Dedicated vs Hosted? Any cross-tenant leakage risks?
[03:18] Liam: No cross-tenant leakage. In hosted we isolate KV per tenancy; in dedicated it's per-pool with guaranteed memory. The difference is eviction pressure: in multi-tenant hosted pools eviction might occur more often under memory pressure. Dedicated gives you predictable cache residency so your long-lived sessions stay hot.
[03:34] Priya: What about large embedding workloads? They can saturate memory. Can KV cache be pinned for certain customers?
[03:40] Liam: On Dedicated we can reserve cache memory; on hosted we have best-effort policies. For your embedding jobs you'd likely schedule batch windows or separate pools to avoid interference.
[03:48] Maya: Quantization — we want to save cost but not drop quality. How does int8 or 4-bit affect latency and output quality?
[03:54] Liam: Quantization reduces memory and can improve throughput since you fit larger batch sizes per GPU. int8 often gives ~1.2-1.5x speedups depending on kernel; 4-bit can give more but with potential quality regressions on some models. We do model-specific calibration and provide quantization profiles. For many open models we've seen negligible quality loss with int8 after calibration; 4-bit sometimes requires eval sets.
[04:17] Jon: Can we do mixed strategy? e.g. int8 for most traffic, fp16 for high-quality responses?
[04:22] Liam: Yes — routing policies let you route to different model variants or quantization levels based on route or rate limits. Also can fallback to higher-precision model when quality checks fail.
[04:31] Maya: About batching — what's the typical latency bump when moving from batch size 1 to batch 8?
[04:35] Liam: It depends on sequence length. For short sequences you may see additional 40-120ms added to individual request latency but tokens/sec overall improves. That said, Redwood's continuous batching aims to fill batches quickly, so with steady QPS it can amortize the waiting time.
[04:48] Jon: Any knobs for max queue time to cap latency?
[04:50] Liam: Yes, we expose a max_queue_ms and target_batch_size; you can set max_queue_ms to keep p99 latency within budget at the cost of lower throughput.
[04:59] Priya: For VPC/on-prem, how is metrics and observability handled? We need per-token cost/latency and traces accessible in our console.
[05:06] Liam: Private deployments ship with a control plane proxy that forwards metrics, or you can run the console in your VPC. Logs and traces can be sent to your telemetry stack (Datadog/CloudWatch). Audit logs, SAML SSO, KMS integration all supported.
[05:18] Carlos: For encryption at rest and in motion, do you support HSM-backed KMS for private?
[05:22] Ava: Yes HSM integrations supported for Private, and Dedicated can use customer-managed KMS via Cloud KMS or on-prem HSM. We'll include the integration guide.
[05:29] [05:29] Speaker 2 (Jon): Edge-case question: noisy neighbor from batch embedding jobs affecting latency — any recommended architectural patterns?
[05:34] Liam: Best practice: separate capacity for batch workloads (dedicated pool or reserved timeslots) and realtime low-latency pools for interactive traffic. For hosted, we offer routing rules to send embedding jobs to a different cluster or queue, reducing interference.
[05:47] Maya: If we commit to Dedicated, what's the lead time to provision? And ability to scale quickly for Black Friday?
[05:53] Ava: Typical lead time is a few days to provision reserved pools in cloud regions; we also support burst capacity options that let you exceed committed capacity during peaks. For on-prem it's project-based and can take longer depending on hardware procurement.
[06:05] Liam: Also worth noting is kernel selection and compilation: we precompile or warm kernels for your pinned model/version to reduce first-request latency. That improves cold-starts substantially.
[06:15] Jon: Are you able to run benchmarks using our exact model repo and weights? We want apples-to-apples comparisons (hosting quant variant vs on-prem fp16).
[06:22] Liam: Yes — we can run a benchmark with your model, quantization variants, and your workload trace. We'll need the model weights and sample inference trace. We'll do hosted baseline, dedicated baseline with your config, and private on-premish sim (if you can't give hardware we'll emulate with equivalent spec).
[06:36] Priya: On compliance, do you keep per-request logs for e-discovery? Retention policy?
[06:41] Ava: We can enable extended audit logs retention as an add-on and provide per-request metadata (route, model version, token counts). We'll share the retention options and costs.
[06:50] Maya: One more — what's the risk profile for model rollouts? If we do canary and a rollback is needed, will we experience hot cache miss spikes?
[06:58] Liam: Canary rollouts can cause cache misses if traffic moves to a variant with empty KV. We mitigate with gradual traffic shifting and pre-warming scripts that replay typical sessions to populate KV before routing large volumes. We'll share a rollout playbook.
[07:14] [07:14] Speaker 1 (Liam): Quick recap of technical recommendations: for strict p99 SLOs go Dedicated or Private with reserved cache memory; use int8 quantization for most traffic after evaluation; separate batch embedding capacity; set max_queue_ms to tune tail latency; prewarm kernels and KV cache before big rollouts; and plan for benchmark runs with your traces.
[07:34] Maya: Sounds good. For numbers, can you provide an expected cost/per-token delta between hosted int8 and dedicated int8? Even a rough estimate would help.
[07:43] Ava: We'll include those in the pricing + perf spreadsheet — rough delta depends on commit level but expect Dedicated to be slightly cheaper per-token at scale due to reserved capacity, but hosted has higher flexibility and lower upfront. We'll quantify with your QPS.
[07:55] Jon: On the benchmarking cadence, what's realistic turnaround? We need a first pass within a week.
[07:59] Liam: If you share traces and model weights by Monday we can do an initial hosted vs dedicated run in 3-5 business days. The private/on-prem sim might add a couple more days.
[08:10] Priya: For the on-prem pilot, what minimal infra specs do you recommend? GPU type, RAM, and NVMe?
[08:15] Liam: For interactive workloads we'd recommend A100 or H100 class for large models; for smaller models 80GB A40-class could work. RAM/CPU depends on sequence lengths; NVMe for fast swap if you use large KV caching or model shards. We'll send a spec sheet.
[08:28] Carlos: Any gotchas around Kubernetes deployments and node autoscaling? We are heavily k8s-based.
[08:33] Liam: Our private runtime can run on k8s; autoscaling needs to be configured conservatively because GPU node provisioning time can be long. We recommend keeping a baseline of warm nodes and scaling with node pools and cluster-autoscaler tuned for GPU.
[08:46] Maya: OK great — let's go ahead with the benchmark playbook.
[08:50] Ava: Perfect — to confirm next steps: Ava will send pricing/bench spreadsheet and SOC2/docs; Liam sends KV cache/batching notes and prewarm scripts; Jon uploads workload trace and success criteria; Priya compiles security checklist. We'll schedule a scoping call for on-prem pilot next week.
[09:05] Jon: Thanks folks, that sounds actionable.
[09:08] Maya: Thanks, appreciate the concrete guidance.
[09:10] Ava: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up via email with links to the docs and proposed times.
\nEnd of transcript.\n\nReferences / Links mentioned during call:
- Dedicated pricing & perf spreadsheet (to be shared)
- KV cache and batching whitepaper (Liam to share)
